pages.title: Scaling thinking by making the model think longer
pages.subtitle: The whole trick in one sentence

blocks.html: In late 2024 OpenAI's o1 showed something startling: if you let a model think longer before answering a hard math or science question, it gets the answer right more often. More test-time compute traded directly for more accuracy. But OpenAI never said how they did it. The whole recipe — the data, the training, the mechanism that controls how long the model thinks — was a black box. This paper asks a deliberately blunt question: what is the simplest possible recipe that reproduces this behavior in the open?

Their answer has two ingredients and nothing else. (1) s1K: a tiny dataset of just 1,000 questions, each paired with a long step-by-step reasoning trace, carefully curated for difficulty, diversity, and quality. (2) Budget forcing: a dead-simple decoding trick that controls thinking length — if you want the model to stop, you force the end-of-thinking token; if you want it to think more, you suppress that token and literally append the word Wait to the transcript, which makes the model second-guess itself and keep reasoning.

Our model s1-32B exceeds o1-preview on competition math questions by up to 27% (MATH and AIME24). Further, scaling s1-32B with budget forcing allows extrapolating beyond its performance without test-time intervention: from 50% to 57% on AIME24.

The headline is the cost asymmetry. The base model is the off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. Fine-tuning it on the 1,000 examples takes 26 minutes on 16 H100 GPUs. No reinforcement learning, no reward models, no million-example datasets — the things everyone assumed o1-style reasoning required. A supervised fine-tune on a thousand examples plus a one-word decoding hack gets you most of the way there.

Why does this matter? It reframes test-time scaling as something cheap and accessible. Two distinct knobs emerge: sequential scaling (one chain of reasoning that gets longer, where later steps build on earlier ones) and parallel scaling (many independent attempts, then majority-vote). The paper argues sequential is the more powerful one, and budget forcing is the simplest way to control it. Everything — model, data, code — was released open-source, which is why s1 became a reference point the moment it appeared.

pages.title: Three filters that turn 59,000 questions into 1,000
pages.subtitle: Quality, Difficulty, Diversity

blocks.html: The naive instinct for teaching reasoning is “more data.” The authors push the opposite bet: a tiny, ruthlessly curated set beats a large noisy one. To make the case they first gather a big pool — 59,029 questions from 16 sources spanning competition math (AIME, MATH), PhD-level science (their own GPQA-style sets), olympiad problems, and brain-teasers — then whittle it down to 1,000 through three sequential filters.

Think of it like assembling a study guide for a brilliant student who only has time for 1,000 problems. You would (1) throw out anything sloppy or malformed, (2) keep only problems that are genuinely hard — easy ones teach nothing — and (3) make sure the survivors cover many different fields, not 1,000 variations of the same integral. That is exactly the pipeline.

Drop anything with formatting errors, broken ASCII art, or non-existent image references; drop questions whose reasoning traces (generated by Gemini Flash Thinking) look garbled. This alone removes roughly 34,000 questions, leaving about 24,000.

A question is only useful for teaching reasoning if it actually requires reasoning. They measure difficulty two ways: a question is kept only if it stumps strong baseline models (Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) — i.e. at least one of them gets it wrong — and they use the length of the reasoning trace as a proxy for difficulty, since a model writing a long chain of thought signals the problem is non-trivial. Easy problems get cut. This drops the pool to about 5,000.

Reading it term by term: $q$ is a candidate question. The left clause asks whether at least one baseline model fails on $q$ — if both already solve it, it teaches nothing and is discarded. The right clause requires the reasoning trace to be at least $\tau$ tokens long, where $\tau$ is a length threshold; a short trace means the problem was trivial. Both conditions must hold ($\land$ is logical AND), so a kept question is one that is both unsolved by a strong baseline and demands a long chain of thought.

From the ~5,000 survivors, classify each question into one of 50 domains (using the Mathematics Subject Classification, plus science fields). Then sample to spread coverage: randomly pick a domain, then within it favor longer-reasoning (harder) problems, repeating until exactly 1,000 remain. The result, s1K, is balanced across fields rather than dominated by whatever topic happened to be most common in the raw pool.

The reasoning traces and answers attached to each of the 1,000 questions are distilled from Google's Gemini Flash Thinking API — so s1K is effectively a 1,000-example transcript of a strong reasoning model's thought process, filtered for the problems most worth learning from.

pages.title: Wait: forcing the model to think longer (or stop)
pages.subtitle: Test-time control with no extra training

blocks.html: Fine-tuning on s1K gives a model that can reason in long chains. But you still need a knob to control how long it reasons at inference time — spend more compute on a hard AIME problem, less on an easy one. Budget forcing is that knob, and it is almost embarrassingly simple: it just edits the decoding stream by adding or removing a special token.

The model's output is split into two phases by special delimiters: a thinking phase (scratch work) ended by an end-of-thinking token, followed by the final answer. Budget forcing manipulates that boundary in two directions.

blocks.text: Forcing it to stop (upper bound on thinking)

blocks.html: If the model has already produced a target number of thinking tokens, force it to stop: append the end-of-thinking token (plus the string Final Answer:) into the stream. This makes the model exit its scratch work early and commit to an answer instead of rambling forever — a cap on test-time compute.

blocks.text: Forcing it to continue (the Wait trick)

blocks.html: The more interesting direction: if you want more thinking, suppress the generation of the end-of-thinking token and instead append the word Wait to the model's current reasoning. Because the model now sees “…Wait” after what looked like a conclusion, it naturally re-examines its own work — often catching an arithmetic slip or a wrong assumption — and continues reasoning. Do this $k$ times to add $k$ rounds of self-correction.

We suppress the generation of the end-of-thinking token delimiter and optionally append the string “Wait” to the model's current reasoning trace to encourage the model to reflect on its current generation.

Concretely: the paper shows a worked example where the model, after appending Wait, revisits a problem about how many letters “r” are in “raspberry,” notices it had miscounted, and corrects itself to the right answer. The word Wait is doing real cognitive work — it is a textual nudge that triggers verification behavior the fine-tuning already taught the model.

Why a literal word and not a learned mechanism? Because it requires zero additional training and works at pure inference time. The authors tried other strings (Hmm, Alternatively) but Wait gave the best gains. It is the laziest possible intervention that works — which is the whole point of the paper's “simple” thesis.

If you are going to claim a method “scales,” you need to define what scaling means precisely. The paper proposes three metrics that any test-time scaling method can be judged on, computed over a set of compute budgets $a \in \mathcal{A}$ (e.g. “think for 2k / 4k / 8k tokens”).

blocks.text: Control — do you actually obey the budget?

blocks.html: Here $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of target compute budgets you asked for, and $|\mathcal{A}|$ is how many there are. For each budget $a$, the indicator $\mathbb{1}(\cdot)$ returns 1 if the actual compute the method used stayed within the requested window $[a_{\min}, a_{\max}]$, else 0. Averaging gives the fraction of budgets the method respected — a method that ignores your budget scores low. Budget forcing achieves 100% control because it directly edits the token stream.

This is the average slope of accuracy versus compute. For every pair of budgets $(a, b)$ with $b > a$, $f(\cdot)$ is the accuracy at that budget, so $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ is the rise in accuracy per extra unit of compute. The sum runs over all $\binom{|\mathcal{A}|}{2}$ pairs and is averaged. A positive, large slope is the whole dream of test-time scaling: each extra token of thinking buys accuracy. A flat or negative slope means thinking longer does not help.

blocks.text: Performance — how high can you get?

blocks.html: Simply the best accuracy the method reaches across any budget. Control and Scaling can be gamed by a method that scales nicely but tops out low; Performance is the ceiling. The ideal method scores high on all three: it obeys budgets (Control), improves with compute (Scaling), and reaches strong absolute accuracy (Performance). Budget forcing's edge is that it is the rare method that gets a perfect Control score while still scaling.

pages.title: s1-32B beats o1-preview — trained in 26 minutes
pages.subtitle: The headline numbers

blocks.html: The test is whether 1,000 examples plus a one-word trick can rival models that reportedly took enormous reasoning-specific training. The recipe: take Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, fine-tune on s1K (the 26-minute, 16-H100 run), apply budget forcing at inference. Call the result s1-32B. Evaluate on competition math (AIME24, MATH500) and graduate science (GPQA Diamond).

Read the first and last rows: the base model scores 26.7% on AIME24, and the same base model after s1K + budget forcing jumps to 56.7% — more than doubling — and lands above o1-preview's 44.6%. On MATH500 it reaches 93.0%, essentially matching o1-preview's 85.5% and approaching full o1. This is the “exceeds o1-preview by up to 27%” claim from the abstract, made concrete.

The most striking result is extrapolation. Without any test-time intervention, s1-32B scores 50% on AIME24. Turning on budget forcing — making it append Wait and keep thinking — pushes it to 57%, a gain bought entirely at inference time with no extra training. The model literally reasons its way past its own default ceiling because you forced it to keep going.
Forcing the model to keep reasoning by appending “Wait” leads to it double-checking its answer, often fixing incorrect reasoning steps.

Sample efficiency matters here too: s1-32B is the most sample-efficient open reasoning model, getting these numbers from 1,000 examples. Compare to contemporaneous distillation efforts that used hundreds of thousands of examples to reach similar territory — s1 reaches the same neighborhood with three orders of magnitude less data.

pages.title: Sequential beats parallel — and Wait beats the alternatives
pages.subtitle: Ablations that explain why it works

blocks.html: Two design choices carry the result, and the ablations isolate each. The first: which word do you append to force more thinking? The second, deeper one: is sequential scaling (one long chain) actually better than parallel scaling (many short chains + majority vote)?

All three nudge words force more thinking, but Wait is the one that reliably converts extra tokens into extra correct answers. The interpretation: Wait most strongly cues the self-correction behavior — it reads like a person catching themselves mid-mistake — whereas Alternatively tends to spawn a fresh (often redundant) approach rather than checking the existing one.

Parallel scaling means sampling many independent answers and taking the majority vote — the classic self-consistency approach. Sequential scaling means one chain that keeps getting longer, where each new step can build on and fix the previous ones. The paper finds sequential scaling has a steeper, longer-lasting slope: budget forcing keeps improving as you add thinking, while majority voting plateaus once the easy-to-agree-on answers are exhausted.

The intuition: majority vote over independent wrong attempts just confirms the same wrong answer many times — there is no mechanism to correct a systematic mistake. A single chain that revisits itself with Wait can catch and repair that mistake, because later reasoning conditions on earlier reasoning. This is the paper's core argument for why the sequential knob is the one worth building on.

One honest limitation the authors flag: budget forcing does not scale forever. Append Wait too many times and accuracy flattens or dips — the model starts looping or over-thinking. Test-time scaling buys you a real but bounded gain; it is a complement to better training, not a replacement.

pages.title: Why s1 became a reference point
pages.subtitle: Reproducing o1 on a budget

blocks.html: When o1 appeared, the prevailing assumption was that o1-style reasoning required massive reinforcement learning over reward models and enormous datasets — something only a frontier lab could afford. s1's contribution is a existence proof that the core behavior is reachable with shocking simplicity: 1,000 curated examples, a supervised fine-tune, and a one-word decoding hack.

items: Data efficiency: 1,000 examples, not millions — quality and diversity beat raw quantity for teaching reasoning.
Compute efficiency: 26 minutes on 16 H100s to fine-tune — reproducible in an afternoon by a small lab.
A clean knob: budget forcing gives 100% control over test-time compute with no training, plus the ability to extrapolate past the model's default accuracy.
Fully open: model, data (s1K), and code released — turning a black-box capability into a community baseline.

blocks.html: It connects directly to several landmark threads. Chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022) showed that prompting a model to think step by step helps; s1 shows you can train and then force that thinking and control its length. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) is the parallel-scaling baseline s1 argues against. And it is the open-source counterpart to OpenAI o1 and the DeepSeek-R1 line, landing in the same window and giving researchers a transparent recipe to study test-time scaling directly.

The lasting idea is the two axes of scaling. For years “scaling” meant train-time scaling — more parameters, more data, more pre-training compute. s1 crisply demonstrates a second axis, test-time scaling, where you spend compute at inference by thinking longer, and shows it can be controlled with something as simple as the word Wait. That framing — that you can buy accuracy after training, on a per-question basis — is the conceptual legacy the paper is cited for.

Trivia worth keeping: the entire fine-tuning dataset is small enough to read — 1,000 problems with their reasoning traces, distilled from Gemini — and the central mechanism is a single English word inserted into the decoding stream. Few influential ML papers have a method this short to state, which is precisely why “just append Wait” became shorthand for the simplest form of test-time scaling.
